events.heading: Supervision requested
events.text: Supervision for Mina Swaab (Jetje’s older sister) is requested, out of fear that the elder sisters might influence her. It is the first moment in the file where Henriette becomes a subject of formal child-protection concern. Around 1928 Mina had become mother of a daughter, Betje (“Bella”); her unknown father was Chinese.

image.caption: Mina Swaab in the state reformatory in Zeist, ca. 1927.

events.heading: “Remove Jetje from home”
events.text: In a confidential conversation with guardian Clasina Kruimel-van Dijk, Mina urgently asked that Henriette (Jetje) be removed from the parental home. “The mother demanded money both before and after Mina’s stay” in the reformatory, the guardian noted; supervision alone, Mina argued, could not be enough to safeguard her. Service in Zandvoort was suggested as the safer alternative.

image.caption: Clasina Kruimel-van Dijk, family guardian of Mina and Henriette Swaab.

events.heading: Guardian visits the family
events.text: Guardian Clasina Kruimel-van Dijk visits the Swaab home in Amsterdam and informs the parents about the children’s situation — institutional oversight entering the family’s own rooms.

events.heading: Jetje must leave home
events.text: The family guardian found Jetje’s parental home far too dirty — no regularity or structure, and street prostitution besides, with the money going to Jetje’s mother. She reported that Jetje had to leave both her family home and her job in Amsterdam.

events.heading: Admitted to Huize Dina
events.text: Henriette Swaab is admitted to Huize Dina. “I have the honour to inform you that Henriette Swaab was brought here yesterday afternoon by her family guardian, Mrs. Kruimel,” Hetta Prins, the directress of Huize Dina, wrote to the juvenile judge — the authorities’ attention now extended from Mina alone to a second Swaab daughter.

image.caption: Girls of Huize Dina doing laundry, ca. 1932.

events.heading: Parents object
events.text: Henriette’s parents were summoned and argued that she had previously been removed from home without reason. They explained her obstinacy in service and said they had reprimanded her sister Sofie. The juvenile judge promised a short stay followed by service near Amsterdam.

events.heading: Competing truths
events.text: Henriette’s mother reported that Jetje was content and well dressed in Amsterdam. Hetta Prins, the directress of Huize Dina, disagreed, and reported to the juvenile judge: “She is a girl whom one does not easily come to know; I am not yet able to form a clear judgment of her character. It seems to me that she is somewhat sly. The girl herself finds it very pleasant here.”

events.heading: Conditional home visits
events.text: Hetta Prins, the directress, decided that Jetje could visit her parents’ home in Amsterdam once every two months — but warned the judge and the guardian that visits would stop if matters did not proceed satisfactorily. Home contact was conditional, and monitored.

events.heading: Mina reprimanded
events.text: Mina (Jetje’s older sister) was reprimanded for corresponding with their sister Sofie, spending a day in Haarlem without permission, and buying unnecessary clothing. Sofie (involved in prostitution) was treated as a risky influence on the younger Swaab sisters.

events.heading: A letter about the mother
events.text: Guardian Kruimel reported that a letter left by Mina suggested the girls’ mother had formerly compelled her daughters to engage in street solicitation. Around the same time, directress Hetta Prins reported that Henriette had begun to improve — but should remain in Santpoort.

events.heading: Stay extended
events.text: Henriette’s detention in Huize Dina is extended for six months. Her parents would have preferred the extension and accepted the decision — a sign of how far institutional care had become the accepted solution.

image.caption: Henriette (Jetje) Swaab, Haarlem, after the war.

events.heading: “More difficult than Mina”
events.text: The family guardian reported that Jetje was much more difficult than her sister Mina and must therefore remain in Huize Dina. The same note recorded that Mina and her future husband were grateful for the care received, and would soon marry.

events.heading: Extended again
events.text: Henriette’s father approved the extension of her stay; her mother insisted that if Jetje married, she should become engaged only to a Jewish young man. On the same date, her stay was extended for six months.

events.heading: Home becomes forbidden
events.text: After a visit to the Swaab family in Amsterdam, directress Hetta Prins decided she could no longer permit Jetje to visit her parental home — not even once every two months. It was too dangerous.

events.heading: Parents lose authority
events.text: The parents were deprived of authority, and guardianship was officially assigned to the Association for the Protection of Jewish Girls — authority shifted from the family to welfare organizations, for Henriette and the wider sibling group.

events.heading: Marriage and loss
events.text: Henriette married Emile Frank in Haarlem in March 1940. He was murdered in Sobibor on 26 March 1943. From Westerbork he wrote her a letter, kept today in the Jewish Museum’s collection — the interwar welfare story cut across by wartime persecution.

events.heading: Michele, and a life after
events.text: Henriette’s daughter Michele Frank was born in Haarlem in December 1943 and survived the war. Henriette remarried James Haverschmidt in 1947; Michele later took his name. Henriette died in Haarlem in 2010.

image.caption: Henriette (Jetje) Swaab with her second husband, J. Haverschmidt, in Haarlem after the war.

events.heading: Liberation
events.text: After five years, the war is over. Mina’s daughter Betje grows up permanently with the Kruimel family in Zandvoort; she never saw her biological mother (who survived the war in hiding) again. Henriette and her daughter Michele survive and begin a new life in Haarlem.

image.caption: Guardian Clasina Kruimel-van Dijk with Mina Swaab’s granddaughter Caroline.
